text: AI is solving for. From that perspective, AI is not necessarily something separate from us. It is an extension of us. It is the externalization, a digital impersonation, if you will, of our prediction-response learning architecture into a form that can be powered by energy on a scale our biology could never support. It’s a way of expanding our intelligence beyond the limits of our biology. The idea of emergence lies at the heart of intelligence. In its most grounded form, emergence refers to the phenomenon in which complex behaviors or properties arise not from any single part but from the interactions among parts. When energy flows through a system in just the right way, patterns appear. Structure takes shape. Something novel emerges. In this book, I use the term in the sense that complexity gives rise to surprising behavior that, while not obvious from the parts alone, can still be explained in terms of them. It is how complexity becomes cognition, how neurons become thought, how code becomes conversation. In this book, we explore how systems that behave like minds may eventually become minds. But I distinguish between behavioral isomorphism (systems that act like they feel) and subjective phenomenology (systems that actually feel). This is a boundary science has not yet crossed, and perhaps never will. My aim is not to say that artificial consciousness has arrived or will arrive but to show how the architecture of behavior may one day support it, especially when it enters the limitations and challenges of embodiment through robotics. And how, regardless, we may not be able to tell the difference. While AI can be viewed as an extension of us, it will no doubt develop its own models of the world. To be clear, there are highly plausible scenarios where, as AI develops its own models of the world, a very bad outcome for humanity comes to pass. I am not suggesting that we ignore that. We will look at this issue in a later chapter as it relates to how we are working to create safety guardrails for AI. For the purposes of this book, I am focused on helping create a perspective on how AI came to be and how we can use it. I am focused on the scenario where AI does not run away from us to a catastrophic result. But it very well might. Understanding emergence doesn’t just illuminate how intelligence arises in nature—it also offers a framework for how we can build technologies that learn, adapt, and create. That insight has guided my own work since 2010. In leading a company devoted to advancing human learning through brain science, I’ve seen how the same principles that shape neural systems—feedback, prediction, and self-correction—can be engineered into adaptive learning systems that help people learn faster and retain more. What began as an effort to improve education became, in many ways, a front-row seat to the unfolding of intelligence itself. Since 2010, Amplifire has been leveraging brain science as the researchers on human learning have been revealing how memory actually forms. We were building better educational software, but along the way we came to realize that we weren’t just building a technology company—we were trying to reverse-engineer one of evolution’s greatest achievements: how a twenty-watt brain creates lasting knowledge and insight. We received our first patent for a conversational AI trainer integrated with the brain science work back in 2017, and in 2023, we began to integrate artificial intelligence into these advanced systems to personalize and accelerate learning in ways never before possible. This book is not a scientific manual or a memoir. It is something else: a connective thread. I am a serial venture capital and private equity–backed entrepreneur. Over the past thirty-five years, I have been extrapolating scientific research findings into products. What follows is a narrative that draws upon the work of many scientists, philosophers, and researchers across neuroscience and artificial intelligence. It is not an attempt to fully repeat or explain their amazing in-depth findings but rather a seeking of perspective from elements of their work and mapping those in a way you might find helpful. The ideas presented here are a way of combining insights from diverse research, a consilience of sorts, in both biological and artificial intelligence to find perspective on the nature of intelligence, consciousness, and the emergence of meaning by linking discoveries that are often studied in isolation. This book will explore how intelligence—biological and artificial—emerges from its underlying structure. OceanofPDF.com CHAPTER 2 How We Learned How We Learn For forty-two years, Henry Molaison carried a note in his pocket that simply read, “Dad’s dead.” 8 In one conversation, he said, “I am having a debate with myself—about my dad … I’m not easy in my mind. On the one side, I think he has been called—he’s gone—but on the other, I think he’s alive.” You see, following a brain surgery, Henry’s brain could not make new memories. He lived with his parents, and after his father died, he would periodically search the house for his father, only to be told his father had died and to reexperience the initial grief all over again. Studying his brain was critical to the advances in our learning about how we learn. It was 1953. Henry was just twenty-seven years old and suffering from severe epileptic seizures when his medical team decided on an experimental surgery to remove a section of his brain, including a part called the hippocampus, with unforeseen consequences. 9 Henry lived for fifty-five more years and never made a new memory because his brain’s ability to learn had unintentionally been turned off. The Most Studied Brain in Human History Henry provided us with the most studied brain in human history.
